statement: What is the smallest number $n$ such that among any $n$ whole numbers there are always two whose squares differ by a multiple of 10?

choices.misconception: I only made the squares agree on division by 5, where squares leave remainder 0, 1 or 4, and forgot that they must also agree on division by 2.
I found the 6 possible last digits of a square but forgot that the pigeonhole principle needs one more number than there are boxes.
I used the 10 possible last digits of the numbers themselves and forgot that I need one more number than there are boxes.
I used the 10 possible last digits of the numbers themselves, not of their squares, and added one.

hints: When do two squares differ by a multiple of 10?
Pigeonhole: the boxes are the possible last digits of a square. Find how many there are, and check that one number in each box really avoids the property.
Squares can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 have squares ending in six different digits.

solutions.reliable: The difference of two squares is a multiple of 10 exactly when the squares have the same last digit. The last digit of a square depends only on the last digit of the number, and the squares of 0 to 9 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1, so the only possible endings are 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and 9: six boxes. Any 7 numbers put two squares in the same box. But 6 numbers are not enough: the squares of 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, which all end differently. So $n = 7$. The transferable idea: the pigeonhole answer is one more than the largest collection that avoids the property, so build that collection to be sure.

whyOnTest: Pigeonhole needs the right boxes: here they are the last digits a square can have, not the last digits of the numbers.
